overview: Wurundjeri people maintain connections with Birrarung and surrounding Country through family, leadership, language and creative practice. Colonial displacement and reserve administration did not end their cultural identity.

items.text: Ngurungaeta leaders Simon Wonga and William Barak advocated for their communities during colonial dispossession. Barak petitioned the Victorian government to retain Coranderrk.
In 1863, Wonga and Barak helped establish Coranderrk, where Wurundjeri and other displaced Kulin people made a community. The station is one part of their history.
William Barak used visual works to communicate Wurundjeri culture. His pictures remain important cultural documents held across several collections.
In 2012, community members used greenstone from Wil-im-ee Moor-ring to make axes, then removed bark from a river red gum to construct a canoe.
Cultural care encompasses landforms, habitats and continuing practices as well as individual objects. Natural landscapes are integral to community identity and wellbeing.
Wurundjeri descendants established their representative corporation in 1985. In 2017, elders addressed Victoria's Parliament in support of protection for Birrarung.

sources.title: Wurundjeri Corporation: Recent History and Present
